content: Endometrial cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy of the female genital tract in developed countries, with the majority of cases being identified at stage 1. Following primary surgical treatment, the use of adjuvant progestagen therapy has been proposed as a strategy to lower the risk of disease recurrence. The objective of this study was to assess the efficacy and safety of adjuvant progestagen therapy in the management of endometrial cancer. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Trials Specialized Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, with the search extending up to April 2009. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating progestagen therapy in women who had undergone surgery for endometrial cancer. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by two reviewers. Survival outcomes for women receiving progestagen therapy versus those who did not were analyzed using pooled risk ratios (RRs) in random-effects meta-analyses. A total of seven trials involving 4556 women were included in the analysis. Of these, three trials exclusively enrolled women with stage 1 disease, while the remaining four included participants with more advanced stages of the disease. A meta-analysis of four trials revealed no statistically significant difference in the five-year mortality risk between women who received adjuvant progestagen therapy and those who did not (RR = 1.00, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.18). This finding remained consistent across single-trial analyses at four and seven years, as well as in one trial that assessed outcomes over all time points using a hazard ratio (HR). Furthermore, there was no significant difference between the progestagen therapy group and the control group in terms of mortality from endometrial cancer, cardiovascular disease, or other intercurrent illnesses. While one trial suggested that progestagen therapy might reduce the risk of disease relapse (HR = 0.71, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.97; five-year RR = 0.74, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.96), another trial found no evidence of a difference in recurrence rates at seven years (RR = 1.34, 95% CI 0.79 to 2.27). In conclusion, there is no evidence to support the routine use of adjuvant progestagen therapy as part of the primary treatment for endometrial cancer. Multiple RCTs have failed to demonstrate a clear benefit of this approach, and as a result, further trials investigating adjuvant progestagen therapy in this context are unlikely to be warranted.
